front: Why were there concerns about Edward VI's age in 1547?
p1: Edward was only nine — it was feared a regent might seize power, as Richard III had done in 1483 during his nephew's minority.
p2: Power of the monarchy relied on the monarch's image - 9 year old boy could not project image of divinely appointed just and military leader.
p3: Henry had left a divided council between reformists and conservatives — Gardiner and Norfolk's fall in 1546 already left it weighted in favour of the reformists. Edward wouldn't be able to control faction.

front: How did Somerset gain and use power?
p1: Edward Seymour, conspiring with William Paget, quickly monopolised power using the dry stamp and the 'unfulfilled gifts' clause of Henry's will. Seymour made himself Duke of Somerset and Lord Protector.
p2: Somerset centralised power against Henry's will of 16 co-equal councillors. Ruled as an autocrat from Somerset House. Denied Edward VI and power - and pocket money!
p3: Somerset positioned himself as the Good Duke - an ally of the ordinary man and a religious reformer. Led English forces against Scotland during the Rough Wooing.

front: How dangerous was faction under Somerset?
p1: In the reign of a minor there was no authority to control faction — disputes could spill over into rebellion or civil war.
p2: Somerset used his position as Lord Protector to increase his personal wealth and power, giving positions to supporters like his brother Thomas Seymour — who he later executed for treason after attempting a coup. Showed the dangerous culture of ambition Somerset had created.
p3: Anti-Somerset Faction developed with reformers and conservatives led by John Dudley, Earl of Warwick, Thomas Wriothesley, Lord Chancellor, and William Paget. Paget and Warwick were former allies of Somerset.

front: Why did Somerset fall from power in October 1549?
p1: Somerset's arrogant leadership created the Anti-Somerset faction — reformers and conservatives including Warwick, Wriothesley and Paget — who blamed him for encouraging the unrest of 1549.
p2: Feeling threatened, Somerset issued a general summons on 5th October for loyal subjects to defend him against the Council — seen as inciting revolt.
p3: Somerset retreated to Windsor Castle but surrendered when the King turned against him, declaring he was being kept prisoner.

front: How did Northumberland consolidate power after Somerset's fall?
p1: Facing conservative opposition, Warwick allied himself with the reformist faction and committed to further religious reform — becoming Lord President of the Council in 1550. Made himself Duke of Northumberland.
p2: Northumberland needed Somerset's voice as a reformist ally. Released him in 1550. However - saw him as a threat so Somerset was executed in 1552 on (likely) fabricated charges of treason.
p3: Northumberland learnt to work more closely with Edward VI - involved him more in running of government as he grew older. Knew that maintaining support of the monarch would be crucial.

front: Why did Northumberland and Edward attempt to alter the succession in 1553?
p1: Edward feared for the survival of his Protestant changes — Mary was a committed Catholic who had refused even his personal appeals to convert.
p2: Northumberland feared his own fall from power when Mary came to the throne, so married his son Guildford Dudley to Jane Grey to control the heir.
p3: Edward's illness progressed before Jane Grey had children, so in his own hand he crossed out 'male heirs' and named Jane Grey directly — giving the Devise a shaky legal basis.

front: Why did the Devise for the Succession fail to prevent Mary's accession?
p1: Mary had a power base in East Anglia where there was significant hatred of Northumberland after Kett's rebellion — she proclaimed herself Queen on 9th July, before the Council's proclamation of Jane on the 10th.
p2: Council never truly believed in Devise - bullied into it by Northumberland. On the march north, Northumberland's army deserted him and Councillors broke ranks for Mary. He retreated to Cambridge and accepted Mary as queen on the 19th.
p3: Mary entered London to rousing popular support — popular legitimacy proved more powerful than legal manoeuvring, and Northumberland, Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley were all later executed.

front: Why did Mary's gender create problems for her rule?
p1: Mary was the first Queen to rule England in her own right — many believed female rulers could not control powerful men, lead soldiers into battle or display the strength a monarch needed. Precedent of Matilda in 12th Century.
p2: John Knox wrote The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women (1558), comparing female rulers to 'the blind leading those who can see'.
p3: Marriage is a serious hurdle - wife expected to obey husband. Has serious consequences if Mary marries an English noble or a foreign prince.

front: How far did Mary's gender actually undermine her authority as queen?
p1: Despite fears, Mary successfully managed her Council throughout her reign — faction was less serious under Mary than under Edward.
p2: During Wyatt's Rebellion Mary stayed in London against her Council's advice and delivered her Guildhall speech to rally the Londoners — proving female rulers could act with strength.
p3: The willingness of Edward and Northumberland to make Jane Grey queen shows gender was seen as less important than religion — concerns about female rule were subordinate to other political calculations.

front: Why was Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain controversial?
p1: A foreign marriage risked an unpopular influx of foreigners, England's entanglement in foreign wars, and xenophobic popular reaction — Wyatt's Rebellion broke out in January 1554 ostensibly in reaction to the marriage.
p2: Philip was Mary's personal choice — championed by Paget — bringing powerful Habsburg alliances as his father Charles V was Holy Roman Emperor. But Edward Courtenay, championed by Gardiner, was the English alternative.
p3: Ultimately the marriage ended unhappily — after Mary's phantom pregnancy, Philip rarely spent time in England. When Mary died he commented he felt 'a reasonable regret'.

front: How was the marriage to Philip designed to limit its dangers?
p1: A treaty was agreed: Philip would be named King but have no power in his own right; no Spaniards would be granted offices or lands in England.
p2: After Mary's death Philip would have no claim to the throne; England would not be entangled in Spain's wars — terms designed to reassure the English political nation.
p3: The treaty ultimately failed to prevent controversy — England was drawn into Spain's war with France, leading to the humiliating loss of Calais in 1558, the last English territory in France.

front: How effectively did Mary manage faction on her Privy Council?
p1: 'Casual councillors' were excluded from key committees in 1554; in 1555 Mary established an 'inner council' so only her most valued advisors were present.
p2: Three key figures dominated: Gardiner (cautious realist), Paget (exceptional administrator) and Cardinal Pole (zealous Catholic). Pole's return in 1554 brought dispute with Gardiner over the pace of restoration.
p3: These struggles were minor and short-lived — Gardiner's death in 1555 ensured Pole's methods won out. For the majority of Mary's reign the Council worked effectively and carried out her wishes.

front: How smooth was the succession of 1558?
p1: Mary died having failed to produce an heir. On her deathbed Mary reluctantly recognised Elizabeth I as successor but asked her to preserve the Catholic faith.
p2: Philip of Spain chose not to press his claim, preferring a Protestant England to a France-aligned Catholic one.
p3: Henry II of France proclaimed Mary Queen of Scots as the true Queen of England - modified Mary Stuart's heraldry to include coat of arms of England.

front: What did Henry VIII's Third Act of Succession and will establish?
p1: 1543 3rd Act of Succession: If Edward died without heirs the throne would pass to Mary then Elizabeth — though the illegitimacy of both was never reversed.
p2: Henry instructed a Regency Council of 16 members, balanced between reformists (Seymour) and conservatives (Gardiner and Norfolk).
p3: There was an 'unfulfilled gifts' clause which allowed Seymour and Paget to conspire and make Seymour Lord Protector.

front: Who were the two candidates for Mary's hand in marriage and why was the choice controversial?
p1: Edward Courtenay, Earl of Devon — championed by Gardiner as a powerful English noble with royal blood who would secure Mary's reign.
p2: Philip of Spain — championed by Paget and Mary's personal choice; his father Charles V was Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain, but it risked a xenophobic popular reaction.
p3: If Mary married an English noble this would lead to division and faction; a foreign prince risked England's entanglement in foreign wars.

front: Who were the three key figures on Mary's Privy Council?
p1: Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester — a long-standing committed Catholic and cautious realist. Had been imprisoned by Edward in 1551.
p2: William Paget — an eminent political survivor and exceptional administrator who had served Henry, Edward and Mary. Not committed to religious change.
p3: Cardinal Reginald Pole — a fiercely zealous Catholic returned from exile. His return in 1554 brought dispute with Gardiner over the pace of restoration — Gardiner stressed caution; Pole favoured persecution.

front: What religious inheritance did Edward VI receive from Henry VIII?
p1: Henry never truly embraced Protestantism — he only embraced changes that brought him money and power, including the Dissolution of the Monasteries.
p2: The 1539 Act of Six Articles confirmed Catholic practices including Transubstantiation and clerical celibacy — England was doctrinally Catholic despite the break with Rome.
p3: The majority of the country, outside London and East Anglia, just wanted to worship as their ancestors had done for a millennium — they did not understand the differences between Catholicism and Protestantism.

front: What did the three stages of the Edwardian Reformation achieve?
p1: Stage 1 — Destruction, 1547: iconoclasm encouraged; Six Articles and Treason Act repealed; Chantries dissolved. The old had to be destroyed before the new could be installed.
p2: Stage 2 — Limbo, 1548–49: First Book of Common Prayer enforced — a vague compromise on Holy Communion that pleased nobody and prompted the Western Rebellion. Repeal of Treason Laws led to multitude of religious preachers.
p3: Stage 3 — Formulation, 1550–53: Second Book of Common Prayer (1552) removed all Catholic practices and confirmed Communion was purely symbolic. Forty-Two Articles drawn up but never passed — Edward died in 1553.

front: How far was England Protestant by 1553?
p1: Just because de jure England was Protestant does not mean de facto this was true — six years was a small amount of time to upend 1,000 years of Catholic worship.
p2: Bishop Hooper's visitations found that of 311 Gloucester clergymen, 171 couldn't repeat the Ten Commandments and 40 couldn't find the Lord's Prayer.
p3: Evidence from wills shows little support for changes outside London and East Anglia — the rapid restoration of Catholicism under Mary suggests traditional religion still retained its popularity.

front: What were Mary's religious aims and why were they difficult to achieve?
p1: Mary aimed to undo religious changes since 1529 — restoring Papal authority, Catholic practices, Transubstantiation and dissolved monasteries — and secure Catholicism's future by marrying and having children.
p2: Advisors were concerned: Gardiner doubted restoring Papal authority; Renard warned against restoring monastic property; even Charles V and the Pope feared she would move too quickly.
p3: Parliament refused to repeal the Act of Supremacy in October 1553, and in April 1554 landowning MPs refused to reinstate the heresy laws until Mary guaranteed ex-monastic land was safe.

front: What was the process of Mary's Counter-Reformation?
p1: First Act of Repeal (1553) reversed Edward's changes immediately. The Royal Injunctions of 1554 restored Catholic practices — Holy Days, processions and ceremonies — and deprived large numbers of married clergy.
p2: The Second Act of Repeal (November 1554) repealed all religious legislation since 1529. However, Mary was forced to compromise on ex-monastic land - not restored to The Church.
p3: Pole's 12 Decrees of 1556 banned absenteeism, pluralism and simony — showing Mary was improving clerical quality, not just restoring Catholicism.

front: Why were the Marian burnings counter-productive?
p1: 284 people were burnt (51 women), mostly in the Protestant strongholds of the south-east. Large numbers attended but there is little evidence the burnings converted anyone — many viewed them as entertainment.
p2: Burnings of Protestant bishop martyrs inspired resistance - Cranmer's burning in 1556 saw him plunge the hand that wrote a recantation of Protestism into the flames first.
p3: c.800 Protestants fled abroad, including many printers who developed an underground propaganda movement — keeping Cranmer's Prayer Book and Foxe's Book of Martyrs in circulation and radicalising the exiles with Calvinist ideas.

front: How far had England returned to Catholicism by 1558?
p1: Edward's short reign meant much of the country, especially the North, had always remained Catholic. Catholic worship returned speedily — unlike Henry and Edward, Mary faced no rebellion purley on the issue of religion.
p2: Mary failed to suppress the Protestant underground movement. 2/3 of printers were Protestant and 19,000 copies of the Second Book of Common Prayer remained in circulation alongside Foxe's Book of Martyrs.
p3: By not producing an heir, Catholicism did not triumph. But the time it took Elizabeth to re-establish Protestantism suggests the Marian restoration had achieved significant de facto change.

front: What happened in Stage 1 — Destruction (1547) of the Edwardian Reformation?
p1: Royal injunctions were issued encouraging iconoclasm in churches across England.
p2: The Six Articles were repealed — removing the Catholic doctrine set out by Henry. The Treason Act was repealed — it was no longer treason to preach dissenting religious views.
p3: The Chantries were dissolved — seen as superstitious forms of Catholic worship, and also bringing in revenue and land for the Crown.

front: What happened in Stage 2 — Limbo (1548–49) of the Edwardian Reformation?
p1: The repeal of the Treason Laws opened a Pandora's Box of radical ideas — Calvinism, Zwinglism and Lutheranism were all being preached, creating confusion.
p2: Cranmer published the First Book of Common Prayer in December 1548 — enforced nationwide by the First Act of Uniformity. It was deliberately vague on Holy Communion and did not please anyone.
p3: The Act of Uniformity encouraged some Protestant practices but many old Catholic practices like belief in Purgatory remained. Iconoclasm was repeatedly encouraged.

front: What happened in Stage 3 — Formulation (1550–53) of the Edwardian Reformation?
p1: A new ordinal (1550) allowed leading Catholic clergy to be replaced with Protestants. A new Treason Act made it an offence to question the Royal Supremacy.
p2: In 1552, Cranmer published the Second Book of Common Prayer — much more radical than the first, removing all Catholic practices and confirming Communion was purely symbolic.
p3: The Forty-Two Articles (1552) outlining the key doctrines of Edward's Church were drawn up but never passed by Parliament — Edward died in 1553. Nevertheless by 1553, de jure England was a Protestant country.

front: What were the main causes of the Great Price Rise in the mid-Tudor period?
p1: Population rise — the Malthusian Crisis: from 1525–1551 the population rose from 2.3 to 3 million. Agricultural productivity could not keep pace, food prices rose, and bad harvests were worsened by the beginning of the Little Ice Age.
p2: Debasement: Henry VIII reduced the precious metal content of coinage to fund wars — prices rose to compensate. Somerset continued debasement to fund the Scottish war, worsening inflation.
p3: Enclosure transformed arable land to livestock farming for the cloth market — producing less food and increasing unemployment. Commonwealth men blamed enclosure and greedy landlords for rack renting and regrating.

front: How far did Somerset's response to socioeconomic problems make the situation worse?
p1: Somerset commissioned John Hales to investigate enclosures in 1548 and imposed a 5% Sheep Tax — raising expectations he could not fulfil.
p2: The Vagrancy Act of 1547 condemned vagrants to two years slavery for a first offence and lifetime slavery for a second — a deeply unpopular measure showing the government's instinct was punishment rather than relief.
p3: Government fundamentally did not understand causes of Great Price Rise beyond enclosure. Debasement continued to fund Scottish war in ignorance of its impact.

front: How serious was the wider unrest of 1549?
p1: 1549 was the 'year of the many-headed monster' — unrest in over half the counties of England, the most widespread of the Tudor period. Kett's captured Norwich; the Western Rebellion besieged Exeter for a month.
p2: Thousands of soldiers were diverted from the Scottish border. The order to execute 3,000 of the Western rebels demonstrates the establishment's fear.
p3: However neither rebellion attempted to march on London — their demands were written politely to Somerset, anger directed at local gentry rather than the Crown. Ultimately both were no match for government force.

front: What were the causes of Kett's Rebellion?
p1: The unrest began when a mob attacked the enclosures of John Flowerdew, who redirected the protest to Robert Kett — another gentleman who had enclosed land and somehow became leader of rebellion.
p2: Rebels' demands centred on enclosure and high rents, and absent or uneducated clergy. Written politely to Somerset assuming his support as the Good Duke.
p3: In Norfolk 6% owned 60% of the land — the rebellion reflected genuine and extreme economic inequality, not just political opportunism.

front: What happened during Kett's Rebellion?
p1: 16,000 rebels met in July 1549, marched on Norwich, camped at Mousehold Heath and stormed the city. Somerset's commissions on enclosure had raised hopes he was the champion of the poor.
p2: Kett's camp was well-disciplined and organised with Kett maintaining order and dispensing justice. No attempt made to march on London.
p3: Warwick arrived with 12,000 well-trained troops from the Scottish war and massacred the rebels at Dussindale — 3,000 killed, 49 leaders executed for treason.

front: What were the causes of the Western Rebellion of 1549?
p1: Resistance to Protestant reforms. Cornishmen more familiar with Latin language than English. William Body murdered for overseeing iconoclasm in Helston in 1548.
p2: The demands were almost entirely religious — drawn up by literate local clergy. Dissmissed new mass as 'Christmas game'. Chant 'Kill all the gentlemen!' at Bodmin, shows economic grievances also existed.
p3: West country also had resentments towards central government. Cornish viewed themselves as a distinct culture, language and nation. Most didn't speak English. 1497 Cornish rebellion had been crushed by Henry VII.

front: What happened during the Western Rebellion?
p1: The rebels besieged Exeter for a month and attacked gentry at St Michael's Mount, Bodmin and Trematon Castle. Local militia failed to suppress revolt.
p2: Government forces of 8,000 led by Lord John Russell defeated the rebels at Sampford Courtenay — over 3,000 executed.
p3: The rebellion failed due to no clear leadership — different sections attacked different targets, unlike the more organised Kett's Rebellion. Cornish language suppressed after this rebellion.

front: What were the causes of Wyatt's Rebellion in 1554?
p1: The ostensible cause was Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain — xenophobic concerns over a foreign marriage, patronage going to the Spanish, and England being dragged into Habsburg wars.
p2: Xenophobia may have masked other causes. The rebellion began in Protestant Kent — part of the plot was to replace Mary with Elizabeth. Many leaders had lost positions at court due to their faith.
p3: The collapse of the cloth trade created unemployment in Kent. Kentish peiple also had long history of rebellions (1381, 1450).

front: How serious a threat was Wyatt's Rebellion to Mary's reign?
p1: Government soldiers deserted Norfolk and joined Wyatt's forces declaring 'We are all Englishmen!', and Wyatt reached the gates of London — if the Londoners had opened the city gates the rebellion could have succeeded.
p2: Courtenay's revealed plot to Gardiner - forced Wyatt's hand in January. French and other three forces did not join rebellion. Rebellion hard to sustain in winter months.
p3: Mary's decisive Guildhall speech secured the Londoners' loyalty who closed the gates to Wyatt. Wyatt and leaders were executed; Elizabeth was imprisoned in the Tower but released after Wyatt refused to implicate her under torture.

front: How serious was the challenge of getting the Religious Settlement through Parliament?
p1: Catholic bishops and lay nobles in the House of Lords threatened to oppose and alter the settlement — particularly objecting to making Elizabeth 'Head of the Church'.
p2: Elizabeth prorogued parliament over Easter 1559, arrested two vocal critics — the Bishops of Lincoln and Winchester — and compromised by adopting the title 'Supreme Governor' instead.
p3: The Settlement passed the House of Lords by just three votes. Elizabeth then removed the Marian bishops when they refused to swear the Oath of Loyalty.

front: How did Puritans attempt to change the Religious Settlement through Parliament?
p1: In 1571 Walter Strickland attempted to alter the Book of Common Prayer to remove vestments and kneeling at communion. Summoned before the Privy Council for infringing the Royal Prerogative, he was barred from parliament.
p2: In 1586 Anthony Cope MP made a radical 'bill and book' proposal — replacing the Book of Common Prayer with the Genevan Prayer Book and removing the episcopacy. Cope and four supporters were sent to the Tower. The bill was defeated.
p3: J.E. Neale (historian) later argued that Cope and Strickland were part of an organised 'Puritan Choir' who were vocal and powerful voice and a pre-curser to the Puritan dominated parliament of the 17th century. Criticised by Elton (historian).

front: How did Puritans challenge the settlement from within the Church?
p1: The Vestiarian Controversy: Puritans despised vestments. Parker compromised in his 1566 Advertisements — but 37 clergymen who refused lost their jobs.
p2: Puritans attempted to alter the 39 Articles in Church Convocation (1563). Anglican articles only passed by one vote - compromise where cermony is more ambiguous but doctrine is clearly moderate.
p3: Bottom-up prophesying and classis movements in 1570s and 1580s attempted to spread Calvinist and Presbyterian ideals amongst clergy. Later suppressed by Whitgift.

front: How did Puritans challenge the settlement through popular appeals?
p1: Cartwright gave Presbyterian lectures at Cambridge in 1570 denouncing Church hierarchy — he lost his professorship.
p2: Field and Wilcox published the 'Admonition to Parliament' (1572) calling for the end of episcopacy. The Marprelate Tracts (1588–89) made vicious attacks on bishops — but alienated moderates.
p3: Separatist movements were suppressed — Robert Browne's 1581 Brownist Church in Norwich, and Henry Barrow and John Greenwood's 1590s movement — the leaders were arrested and executed in 1593.

front: Why was the Catholic threat limited in the first decade of Elizabeth's reign?
p1: Elizabeth's tolerance — the sole recusancy punishment was a 1 shilling fine. Many Church Papists attended Church of England services before attending secret Catholic services. Elizabeth 'would not open windows unto men's souls'.
p2: Philip of Spain persuaded Pope Pius IV not to excommunicate Elizabeth in 1563 — Philip feared France gaining control of England if Mary Queen of Scots came to the throne.
p3: Elizabeth resisted parliament's attempts to increase punishments of Catholics. Law that stated those refusing oath of supremacy twice could be executed - Elizabeth decreed that no one would be asked twice!

front: How did seminary priests and Jesuits transform the Catholic threat from the 1570s?
p1: William Allen's 'English College' at Douai trained seminary priests, who arrived in England from 1574. By 1585, 279 had travelled to England. .
p2: From the 1580s Jesuits also arrived — around 650 in total, sheltered by Catholic gentry in priest holes.
p3: Presence in England undermined Elizabeth's goal for Catholicism to 'wither on the vine'. New generation of priests are revitalising the religion - network of priest holes in gentry and noble homes particularly undermining.

front: What problems faced the Catholics 1559-1589?
p1: Government legislation was effective. Initial tolerance ensured majority of Catholics conformed. Later reprisals and increase in executions were effective.
p2: Foreign support was weak. 1570 excommunication was too little, too late. Habsburg-Valois rivalry prevented coordinated Catholic action until late in the 1580s. The failure of the Spanish Armada in 1588 was a major propaganda boost for Protestantism.
p3: Elizabeth's 45-year reign was decisive — the Catholic establishment from Mary's reign died out and the new generation of gentry, nobility and clergy all grew up under Elizabeth's settlement.

front: What domestic religious pressures did Elizabeth face in 1558?
p1: Returning Marian exiles had been radicalised by Calvinist and Zwinglian ideas in Zurich, Frankfurt and Geneva — denying any role for the monarch in the Church.
p2: The powerful bishops Elizabeth inherited from Mary were all Catholics. Approximately 1/3 of the powerful English nobility and gentry retained the Catholic faith privately.
p3: Under Mary's reign Catholicism had been restored by law. Elizabeth's personal beliefs: raised Protestant but found radical Protestantism tedious and had a fondness for ceremonial aspects of Catholicism.

front: What international religious pressures did Elizabeth face in 1558?
p1: Spain and France were both strongly Catholic. The Habsburg-Valois rivalry meant they despised each other — Elizabeth's political future depended on this rivalry continuing.
p2: Scotland was a complication — Mary Queen of Scots was married to the French Dauphin Francis. Henry II of France presented Mary as the true Queen of England — a figure unifying Scotland, France and England against Elizabeth.
p3: Many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce. In 1559 Scottish Protestant Lords overthrew Mary of Guise and made Scotland Protestant.

front: What were the key provisions of the Act of Supremacy (1559)?
p1: Removed the Pope's authority over the English Church. Made Elizabeth Supreme Governor of the Church — not 'Supreme Head' as Henry had been, to avoid offending those who believed a woman could not be Head of the Church.
p2: Elizabeth was in charge of a strict episcopal hierarchy of Archbishops and Bishops.
p3: All clergy and royal officials had to swear oath of loyalty to Elizabeth. Parliament tried to enforce capital punishment for those who refused but Elizabeth did not enforce this.

front: What were the key provisions of the Act of Uniformity (1559)?
p1: Cranmer's 1552 Book of Common Prayer used in all churches — but the 'Black Rubric' that explicitly denied Transubstantiation was omitted, leaving the question deliberately ambiguous.
p2: Visitations would take place by bishops to ensure all churches were following the style of the Church of England as set out in Royal Injunctions.
p3: Everyone must attend a licensed Church of England church on a Sunday — recusancy fine of 1 shilling (average weekly wage of a labourer).

front: What did the Royal Injunctions of 1559 establish?
p1: Church taxes (First Fruits and Tenths) were to be paid to the Crown. The few small monasteries that Mary had managed to restore were dissolved again.
p2: The clergy were to wear distinctive vestments. Clergy could marry. Music was encouraged at services and images (statues and stained glass) were accepted.
p3: Elizabeth described the settlement as Via Media — 'the middle way' — designed to be an acceptable compromise that would cease religious conflict.

front: What were Matthew Parker's key actions as Archbishop (1559–75)?
p1: Parker had previously been Anne Boleyn's chaplain — a Protestant who had not gone into exile during Mary's reign and was not radicalised by Calvinism or Zwinglism.
p2: Parker defended the Religious Settlement by overseeing the passage of the 39 Articles at the Convocation of 1563 — resisting Puritan attempts to introduce more radical changes. These changes were defeated by a single vote.
p3: Parker reached a compromise with Puritans during the Vestiarian Controversy in his 1566 Advertisements — conceding that clergy could wear simply a 'comely surplice with long sleeves' at Communion.

front: What were Grindal's and Whitgift's key actions as Archbishop?
p1: Edmund Grindal (1575–83): a former Marian exile sympathetic to Puritan concerns. Came into conflict with Elizabeth over prophesyings — ordered to suppress them in 1576, he refused. Suspended in 1577 and confined to house arrest until his death in 1583.
p2: John Whitgift (1583–1604): used the Court of High Commission to root out non-conformists. Used the Three Articles as a test — clergy had to swear Elizabeth had sovereignty over Church matters, the Book of Common Prayer was the only one to be used, and the 39 Articles were agreeable to God.
p3: Around 300 Puritan clergy were removed by Whitgift's methods. Whitgift showed determined repression could contain but not eliminate the Puritan challenge — Elizabeth supported Whitgift and died holding his hand.

front: What were the events of the Rising of the North (1569–70)?
p1: A plot to marry Mary to the Duke of Norfolk to strengthen her claim to the English throne was uncovered. The Catholic northern earls of Northumberland and Westmoreland launched an uprising.
p2: The rebels captured Durham and held Catholic Latin mass in the Cathedral. A summons was issued to other Catholic nobility and gentry — none answered the call.
p3: A royal army led by the Earl of Sussex marched north and the rebels fled without fighting a battle. Mary was moved to Coventry. Elizabeth executed 450 rebels.

front: What was the significance of Mary Queen of Scots' arrival in England and the Papal Bull of 1570?
p1: Mary Queen of Scots was forced to abdicate in 1567 following suspected involvement in the assassination of Lord Darnley. In 1568 Mary fled to northern England seeking Elizabeth's support — placed under house arrest.
p2: Mary was a real danger — Elizabeth's cousin, next in line, and if she succeeded she would likely restore Catholicism. Her arrival in the highly Catholic North provided a figurehead around which Catholic plots would ferment.
p3: In 1570, Pope Pius V issued his Papal bull Regnans in Excelsis excommunicating Elizabeth — Catholics were now absolved of any loyalty to her. This transformed the Catholic threat from passive non-conformity to active potential treachery.

front: What were the three main Catholic plots against Elizabeth?
p1: 1571 — Ridolfi Plot: Catholic banker Ridolfi plotted with the Pope, Philip II and the Duke of Norfolk to marry Mary to Norfolk and provoke a Catholic uprising. Discovered by Cecil. Norfolk executed 1572 but Elizabeth resisted calls to execute Mary.
p2: 1583 — Throckmorton Plot: involving the Duke of Guise, Philip II, the Pope and William Allen's seminary priests. Uncovered by Walsingham's spies. Led to Bond of Association (1584) - Privy Council agree to execute anyone associated with future plots (Mary QoS).
p3: 1586 — Babington Plot: plot involving Elizabeth's assassination and Spanish-French invasion. Walsingham discovered evidence directly implicating Mary herself. Parliament petitioned for Mary's execution — she was executed in February 1587.

front: How did the government targeted seminary priests and Jesuits?
p1: Walsingham's spies worked to investiage and discover missionary priest networks. Priests were tortured until more names revealed.
p2: 1581 — recusancy fines increased to £20 a month; converting someone to Catholicism became treason. 1585 — all Catholic priests expelled from England; anyone found harbouring a priest to be executed.
p3: 133 seminary priests and Jesuits were executed as a result of the 1585 legislation.

front: How effectively did Elizabeth manage faction on her Privy Council?
p1: Elizabeth stayed aloof of faction and encouraged disputes to get wider debate. By delaying decisions she showed favour to no particular faction. She used her gender to manage loyalty — councillors competed for her affection (particularly Leicester and Cecil).
p2: 1565–66: Leicester came into dispute with Norfolk and Sussex over Amy Robsart's death. Factions wore identifying ribbons at court - almost ended in violence. Elizabeth ended it by making clear she would not marry Leicester.
p3: 1578–85: the Dutch Revolt divided the Council — Leicester and Walsingham urged intervention; Burghley counselled caution. Elizabeth refrained from siding until the assassination of William of Orange in 1585 forced her hand. Faction potentially weakened foreign policy.

front: Why did Elizabeth refuse to marry or name a successor?
p1: Elizabeth resented sharing power with a man and described naming a successor as 'buried alive' — it would mean enemies developing plots around that successor. As she grew older, key ministers would abandon her for a named successor.
p2: The choice was almost impossible: a fellow monarch risked foreign entanglement as Mary I's marriage to Philip had proved; foreigners were unpopular; an English noble could create resentment and faction; almost all candidates were Catholic.
p3: Elizabeth's personal experience of marriage also mattered. Her parents' marriage ended in execution. Her sisters' in rebellion. Also likely suffered sexual abuse from Thomas Seymour as a teenager which shaped attitudes of men.

front: What was the impact of Elizabeth's refusal to resolve the succession question?
p1: In 1579 John Stubbs wrote a pamphlet criticising the Alençon match — Elizabeth had all copies burned and his right hand removed. The crowd described Stubbs as 'a true Englishman', showing public support for his position.
p2: The Bond of Association (1584) pledged to kill anyone linked to future plots against Elizabeth. Combined pressure of Lords, Commons and Privy Council following the Babington Plot forced Elizabeth's hand — Mary was executed in 1587.
p3: Despite never naming a successor, Elizabeth's tacit acknowledgement that James VI would succeed meant the issue was ultimately manageable. The peaceful succession of James I in 1603 vindicated Elizabeth's long-term strategy.

front: What were the powers of the Elizabethan monarch?
p1: The monarch was believed to derive power directly from God. All legislation had to be approved by the monarch's Royal Assent — the monarch had every right to veto legislation.
p2: The monarch could issue Royal Proclamations, had the power to call, prorogue and dissolve parliament at will, and presided at Court surrounded by courtiers.
p3: The Royal Prerogative covered matters only the monarch could decide: religion, war, the succession and foreign policy.

front: What were the roles of the Privy Council and Parliament?
p1: The Privy Council was the council of the monarch's most important advisors — maximum 20 members. Met several times a week. Key figures included the Secretary of State and Lord Treasurer. Dominated for most of the reign by William Cecil.
p2: Parliament could pass legislation which was more permanent and enforceable than a proclamation. The monarch needed the approval of parliament to gain taxation. Called ten times during Elizabeth's reign.
p3: The House of Commons tended to be members of the gentry. The House of Lords included Lords Temporal (nobility) and Lords Spiritual (26 bishops). Legislation had to be approved by both houses before being sent for Royal Assent.

front: Who was William Cecil and what did he achieve?
p1: Cecil was Elizabeth's principal advisor until his death in 1598. He held the posts of Secretary of State until 1572, then Lord Treasurer from 1572 to his death.
p2: He helped draft the Religious Settlement, managed Elizabeth's correspondence, created an intelligence service to discover plots and ran the Privy Council. He became Lord Burghley in 1571.
p3: Cecil was by nature a cautious and pragmatic man whose prudence often aligned with Elizabeth's instincts on difficult decisions — he was the most important figure in Elizabethan government.

front: Who were Robert Dudley, Walsingham and Norfolk?
p1: Robert Dudley (Earl of Leicester from 1564): Elizabeth's favourite — tall, handsome, charismatic. Promoted more for personality than political skill. His wife Amy Robsart died in mysterious circumstances in 1560. A devout Puritan who championed military intervention to protect Protestants abroad.
p2: Sir Francis Walsingham: a protégé of Cecil. Took over the spy network and Secretary of State in 1573. A devout Puritan who witnessed St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572) and feared international Catholic conspiracy.
p3: Thomas Howard, Duke of Norfolk: the only Duke in England, raised Protestant but with strong Catholic familial links. Executed in 1572 for his role in the Rising of the North and Ridolfi Plot.

front: What specific tools and methods did Elizabeth use to control Parliament?
p1: Elizabeth could dissolve a parliament she disapproved of and call a new one with newly elected MPs, or prorogue parliament — suspending it while pressure was put on MPs to change position.
p2: Elizabeth and the Privy Council influenced the choice of Speaker, who controlled debates. If a disapproved bill passed both Houses, Elizabeth could use her Royal Veto. As a last resort, she could arrest MPs challenging her prerogative as traitors.
p3: The Privy Council were expected to promote Elizabeth's wishes in Parliament — many Councillors were prominent politicians who dominated parliamentary business.

front: What were the main parliamentary conflicts over religion and freedom of speech?
p1: Catholic Lords and Bishops attempted to block Act of Supremacy in parliament of 1559 - defeated after Easter prorogation and suspension of two bishops.
p2: Puritans: Strickland's Bill (1571) and Cope's 'bill and book' (1586) both attempted to alter the Religious Settlement — blocked as infringements of the Royal Prerogative.
p3: Wentworth brothers criticised Elizabeth's denial of Parliament's rights to discuss marriage and the succession (1566, 1571, 1576, 1587, 1593) — in 1576 Peter Wentworth compared Elizabeth to 'the work of the devil'. Sent to Tower by rest of House - isolated figure.

front: What were the parliamentary conflicts over marriage and Mary Queen of Scots?
p1: Many MPs feared that if Elizabeth died unmarried the throne would pass to the Catholic Mary Queen of Scots. Elizabeth was presented with petitions to marry in 1559 and 1563.
p2: 1566 Parliament: following Elizabeth's near-fatal Smallpox in 1562, demand to marry was attached as condition to subsidy bill. Elizabeth reduced her subsidy by 1/3 to appease Parliament but reaffirmed the succession was part of her Royal Prerogative.
p3: Parliament was vehemently hostile to Mary QoS and pushed for her execution for many years. Following the Babington Plot, Parliament petitioned Elizabeth — combined pressure of the Lords, Commons and Privy Council forced Elizabeth's hand. Mary was executed in 1587.

front: Who were Elizabeth's main suitors?
p1: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester — perhaps Elizabeth's personal preference. He would have been a scandalous choice — his father, brother and grandfather had all been executed as traitors. Amy Robsart's death was source of gossip.
p2: Habsburg match: Archduke Charles of Austria — promoted by Cecil in 1567 as a key ally but his Catholicism was a problem. Philip II of Spain — he proposed in 1559 but this would have been a wildly unpopular choice.
p3: Francis, Duke of Alençon — the only foreign suitor who came in person in 1579. Extremely charming and Elizabeth was very fond of him despite being 23 years younger than her. He was not particularly committed to Catholicism — but died in 1584.

front: What was the role of gender in Elizabethan government?
p1: Elizabeth used her gender as a political tool — courtiers and councillors competed for her affection, giving her leverage over faction that a male monarch would not have had.
p2: However gender created real problems: Parliament and the Privy Council assumed a queen would need a husband to support her rule, generating persistent pressure to marry. Elizabeth's gender was used to justify demands that she name a successor.
p3: Marriage was a key method of forging foreign alliances — a male monarch could have married Archduke Charles of Austria to secure a powerful Habsburg ally without domestic controversy. Elizabeth could not do this without risking a co-ruler who would effectively share sovereignty.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What was the financial situation Elizabeth inherited in 1558?
p1: Elizabeth inherited a debt of £227,000 from Mary's involvement in the war with France, largely owed to the Antwerp Exchange at 14% interest. Gresham identified three problems: debasement of coinage; cost of war; and the Hanseatic League's control over wool exports.
p2: Mary had introduced the revised Book of Rates which boosted customs revenue, and the Exchequer now collected three-quarters of Crown revenue. Elizabeth inherited able administrators in Gresham and Lord Treasurer William Paulet.
p3: Gresham's advice was to maintain an excellent credit rating by swiftly repaying debt and avoiding loans in peacetime — allowing Elizabeth to raise loans quickly at favourable rates when war made it necessary.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How successfully did Elizabeth manage the Crown's finances before 1585?
p1: Elizabeth effectively removed the Marian debt. By 1576 the Chancellor of the Exchequer informed parliament that the Marian debt had been removed. By 1584 Elizabeth had accrued a surplus of £300,000.
p2: She achieved this by not indulging in the excessive lifestyle of her father, not spending on lavish building projects, going on 'progress' each summer at courtiers' expense, and avoiding war at all cost.
p3: However she sold a significant portion of Crown Lands — bringing in £600,000 but depleting long-term income. Custom Farmers led to widespread corruption that reduced actual revenues below their potential. Refused to pay for professional tax-collecting service.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What caused inflation during Elizabeth's reign?
p1: Population rise from c.2.7 to c.4 million between 1547 and 1603 meant demand outstripped supply. Poor harvests — made common by the Little Ice Age — reduced supply further. By the 1560s, average food prices were triple those of Henry VII's reign.
p2: Bullion: gold and silver from the New World reduced the value of precious metals across Europe — making coinage less valuable and pushing up prices.
p3: Contemporaries blamed enclosure and greedy landlords — they did not understand how rising population affected supply and demand. This misdiagnosis meant the government could not tackle the underlying cause.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How effectively did overseas trade develop in Europe and the Middle East?
p1: Cloth trade represented 75% of exports at start of reign. The Dutch Revolt and war with Spain collapsed the Antwerp cloth market — new markets were needed. New companies were established: Muscovy Company (1555); Eastland Company (1579); Levant Company (1580); East India Company (1600).
p2: Muscovy Company (1555) founded to trade in Russia - over time became prosperous trading cloth for Russian hides. Eastland Company (1579) established to trade in Baltic less successful due to dominance of German Hanseatic League.
p3: Levant Company (1580) founded to trade in Eastern Mediterranean with Ottomans. Attempts to build trading relationship with Shah of Persia failed for religious reasons.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How effectively did overseas trade develop in the Americas and Asia?
p1: Americas dominated by Spain and Portugal. Raleigh's colonisation attempts at Roanoke island fail in 1580s. John Dee and Martin Frobisher fail to find north-west passage.
p2: John Hawkins establishes English involvement in Transatlantic Slave Trade (1562) - still dominated by Spanish and Portuguese in this period.
p3: East India Company established 1600 - would go on to become vital to empire but too early for Elizabeth I to benefit. By end of reign 75% of trade is with traditional European partners.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What caused poverty and vagrancy to grow during Elizabeth's reign?
p1: The growing population (3 to 4 million) created Malthusian Crisis — employers could lower wages while landlords raised rents. Combined with inflation this created large amounts of poverty.
p2: The wars with Spain and Ireland compounded the problem — soldiers and sailors were discharged far from home, often with no pay and serious injuries, adding to the pool of destitute vagrants.
p3: Contemporaries blamed enclosure and greedy landlords. By 1600, in some areas over 70% of available arable land was enclosed - but nationally only 2%.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How did government attitudes to poverty change at the start Elizabeth's reign?
p1: Distinction made between deserving and undeserving poor. Early legislation only supported deserving - e.g. 1563 Alms Act created voluntary poor rate.
p2: Belief that undeserving poor needed regulating, not helping. 1563 Statute of Artificers set maximum wage rates and enforced 7-year apprenticeships. 1572 Vagabonds Act set physical mutilation as punishmend for vagrancy.
p3: Poor relief was domain of church, not state. Early examples of poor relief are either run at parish level, or are voluntary poor rates. JPs take over later in reign.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: Who were Gresham and Paulet and what financial advice did they give?
p1: Elizabeth inherited a debt of £227,000 from Mary's involvement in the war with France — largely owed to the Antwerp Exchange at an interest rate of 14%.
p2: Gresham identified three major problems: debasement of coinage begun under Henry VIII; the cost of war and damaging loans; the Hanseatic League's control over the export market for English wools.
p3: Mary had introduced the revised Book of Rates determining customs duties and the Exchequer now collected roughly three-quarters of Crown revenue — giving Elizabeth a better administrative base than Mary had inherited.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How did Gresham and Paulet improve royal finances?
p1: Sir Thomas Gresham: a highly perceptive financier experienced in the key money markets. Stopped debasement and led the recoinage efforts of 1560-1.
p2: In 1565 Gresham founded the Royal Exchange as a London equivalent to the Antwerp Exchange. Cecil eventually agreed to his argument that relaxing usury laws would stimulate the English financial markets.
p3: William Paulet: a highly effective and experienced Lord Treasurer. Excellent financial management helped Elizabeth clear Marian debt by 1576.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What were ordinary and extraordinary revenue and how did Elizabeth exploit them?
p1: Ordinary revenue was received by default every year: Crown lands, Customs Duties, profits from justice, Church revenue (First Fruits and Tenths). Elizabeth increased Crown land revenues from £86,000 to £111,000 though sold significant portions.
p2: Customs Duties: Mary's revised Book of Rates boosted revenue — from £29,315 to £82,797 in one year. However the Book of Rates was not regularly revised and by the 1590s customs revenue stood at only £91,000.
p3: Extraordinary revenue: parliamentary grants of subsidies (around £100,000) and fifteenths and tenths (around £30,000). Taxes in England were amongst the lowest in Europe — local gentry who made assessments undervalued their own and their lord's lands.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What were the specific causes of inflation?
p1: Population rise: between 1547 and 1603 the population increased from c.2.7 million to c.4 million. The availability of resources could not increase at the same rate — increased demand led to increased prices. By the 1560s, average food prices were triple those of Henry VII's reign.
p2: Poor harvests — made common by the Little Ice Age — decreased the supply of goods and thus increased prices.
p3: Bullion: huge quantities of gold and silver from the New World decreased the value of precious metals — coinage became less valuable and prices rose.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How did the government attempt to tackle inflation?
p1: Gresham attempted recoinage in 1560 — calling in debased coins and removing the base alloys. By 1561 the debased coins had been called in — but prices did not go down. Merchants simply set the same prices, or higher.
p2: Elizabeth encouraged her people to limit demand by encouraging fasting during Lent and 'fish days' on Wednesdays and Fridays. The 1586 Book of Orders prohibited hoarding of grain.
p3: Ultimately the government could not tackle the issue — they did not understand how rising population affected supply and demand. Inflation was a structural problem no Tudor government had the economic tools to solve.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What was the cost of the war with Spain from 1585?
p1: The Treaty of Nonsuch committed Elizabeth to £126,000 per year to support the Dutch rebels. In total the war cost £4.5 million — £2m in the Netherlands, £2m in Ireland, £500,000 supporting Henry of Navarre and £160,000 defending against the Spanish Armada.
p2: Even before 1585 the ongoing Dutch Revolt negatively affected English trade. A 1576 mutiny by Spanish troops in Antwerp destroyed much of that city — a centre for the English wool trade. Elizabeth's seizure of the Genoese Leon in 1568 prompted a trade embargo with Spain until 1573.
p3: Elizabeth's hard work at improving her finances was made redundant by the war. Her surplus of £300,000 was used almost entirely in the first year. Elizabeth was forced to sell more Crown lands in the 1590s and resort to monopolies as patronage — contributing to price rises and creating dissatisfaction in Parliament.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What economic benefits did the war with Spain bring?
p1: Many Flemings fled the Netherlands in 1566 and brought improved manufacturing skills to England — particularly cloth-making. French Huguenots fleeing persecution also brought manufacturing skills and trade to England.
p2: Elizabeth's sponsorship of privateers often brought dividends — Drake's circumnavigation of the globe (1577–80) stole £400,000 from Spanish ships and ports. His 1587 raid on Cadiz brought £140,000.
p3: Due to the cost of war, Elizabeth resorted to monopolies in her later years to reward her courtiers — these contributed to price rises and caused great dissatisfaction. Elizabeth forced to sell more Crown lands in the 1590s, further weakening long-term royal finances.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How did government attitudes to poverty shift in Elizabeth's later reign?
p1: 1576 Act for the Relief of the Poor: 'able-bodied' poor would be provided work, often in a House of Correction — the first example of the state recognising the 'undeserving poor' also require help, not just punishment.
p2: 1598 Act for the Relief of the Poor: begging was forbidden. JPs now appointed materials to employ the able-bodied poor. 1598 Act for the Punishment of Rogues, Vagabonds and Sturdy Beggars: 'sturdy beggars' to be whipped and returned to their place of birth.
p3: 1601 Poor Law: the government assumed responsibility for providing the Poor Rate from the Church. The distinction between 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor was codified. These provisions lasted until the mid-19th century.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What local responses to poverty existed and how effective were they?
p1: Norwich, influenced by the experience of Kett's rebellion, banned begging. Instead the wealthiest citizens regularly contributed to a fund to support the poorest.
p2: Ipswich, Exeter and Cambridge all introduced similar schemes. Many wealthy individuals contributed to the poor by bequeathing funds in their wills.
p3: Archbishops Parker and Whitgift contributed to almshouses; Leicester established a hospital for the poor in Warwick. However these efforts were ultimately limited and no replacement for effective central legislation.

front: What was the financial impact of the war with Spain?
p1: The £4.5 million cost destroyed Elizabeth's surplus almost immediately. She was forced to sell more Crown lands and resort to monopolies as patronage — contributing to price rises and creating dissatisfaction in Parliament.
p2: Changed Elizabeth's need for taxation - but parliament willing to provide. Double subsidy in 1589 and triple subsidy secured in 1593!
p3: Victory against the Armada came at huge cost — forced loans of £75,000 from the nobility and £56,000 from the City of London.

front: What caused the socioeconomic crisis of the 1590s?
p1: A series of bad harvests from 1594–98 doubled the average price of wheat. The Malthusian Crisis continued — population continued to outstrip food production. The death rate increased by 50% at the peak of the crisis in 1595–7.
p2: The wars with Spain and Ireland compounded the problem: unprecedented taxation in 1589 and 1593; monopolies raising prices; discharged soldiers adding to the numbers of destitute vagrants.
p3: Between 1595–98 food riots erupted in Kent, Sussex, Somerset and Norfolk. Elizabeth's granting of monopolies to favourites increased prices on staple goods..

front: How effectively did the government respond to the socioeconomic crisis of the 1590s?
p1: The Oxfordshire Rising of 1596 — a protest against enclosure at the peak of the food crisis — was quickly suppressed. The five ringleaders were executed. In the end only four people actually turned up..
p2: The 1597 Tillage Act reversed enclosure carried out since 1588. The 1601 Poor Law codified the distinction between 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor and made the state permanently responsible for poor relief — lasting until the mid-19th century.
p3: The crisis revealed the structural limits of Elizabethan government — it could respond to disorder but not prevent its underlying causes.

front: What were the key events of the Spanish Armada (1588)?
p1: Philip II sent a fearsome invasion force of 130 ships and 57,000 men. The English used fireships at Calais to scatter the Armada. The Battle of Gravelines inflicted significant Spanish losses.
p2: Storms destroyed over half the remaining fleet off Scotland and Ireland. Victory was a major propaganda boost — Elizabeth encouraged the belief that God had intervened on her side with a medal 'God blew, and they were scattered'.
p3: Elizabeth's role in the Armada, leading her army in full armour with her famous Tilbury speech, demonstrated her strength and leadership: 'I know I have the body of a weak, feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king.'

front: What happened in the war with Spain after the Armada?
p1: At sea, failure was common after 1588 — Drake's 'English Armada' of 1589 against Spain was an unmitigated disaster. English attempts to capture the treasure fleet routinely failed.
p2: The English capture of the Madre de Dios in 1592 brought riches worth half the Crown's usual income. English support for the Dutch rebels ensured their survival and eventual success.
p3: The Huguenot Henry of Navarre's coronation as Henry IV in 1589 seemed a huge opportunity — Elizabeth sent gifts of £20,000 and 10,000 troops. However his conversion to Catholicism and unilateral peace with Spain in 1598 negated these gains.

front: What were the key issues in Parliament during Elizabeth's later years — monopolies and purveyance?
p1: Monopolies: since Elizabeth no longer had funds to bestow lavish gifts on her favourites, she resorted to granting monopolies. The holder had the sole right to selling that good in England. Raised as a major issue in the Parliament of 1597.
p2: In the 1601 Parliament MPs publicly listed the monopolies granted since 1597 — one MP sarcastically commented 'is not bread there?' Elizabeth recognised the need for concessions, annulling the most contentious monopolies including salt and starch. She used her Golden Speech to appease MPs' anger.
p3: Purveyance — the monarch's customary right to purchase goods at below market value — was criticised by MPs in the 1589 and 1593 Parliaments. Lord Burghley defended it as part of the Royal Prerogative. Elizabeth privately agreed to investigate but no major concessions were made.

front: What were the key parliamentary issues in the later years — succession and taxation?
p1: As Elizabeth entered her 60s in the 1590s, Parliament's attention returned to the succession. Peter Wentworth MP wrote a pamphlet calling on Parliament to be given the right to examine candidates. In 1591 Wentworth was questioned by the Privy Council and imprisoned briefly. He was sent to the Tower in 1593 where he stayed until his death in 1596.
p2: Five of Elizabeth's ten Parliaments were called after 1585 — the war with Spain forced reliance on parliamentary subsidies.
p3: Despite the increased reliance on Parliament, the war provided a common enemy around which Crown and Parliament united. In 1589 Parliament granted a double subsidy. Burghley secured a triple subsidy in 1593.

front: What was the background to Ireland and what caused Tyrone's Rebellion?
p1: The English Crown had laid claim to Ireland since the 12th century — but by the 16th century English power was only truly felt in the Pale around Dublin.
p2: Ulster and Connaught in North/West were ruled by Gaelic chieftans - opposed to English culture. Munster and Leinster in South/East were ruled by autonomous Anglo-Norman families who resented control from London. All were Catholic.
p3: Throughout Elizabeth's reign Ireland was a source of unrest — the Fitzgerald Rebellions of 1569–73 and 1579–83. Elizabeth had attempted to increase control through plantations in Munster - unsuccessfully.

front: What happened during the Nine Years' War?
p1: 1594 - Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone starts rebellion of Gaelic chieftans against English rule. Victory at Yellow Ford in 1598 saw Tyrone control majority of island.
p2: 4,000 elite Spanish troops arrive to support siege of Kinsale in 1600. Spanish army on England's doorstep!
p3: Lord Mountjoy eventually defeats Spanish at Kinsale (1601) and secures surrender of Tyrone in 1603.

front: How serious a problem was Tyrone's Rebellion?
p1: Rebellion extremelly costly to suppress - over £2 million. Crippling in context of war with Spain. Yellow Ford defeat was a humiliation.
p2: In 1599, the Earl of Essex led an English force of 16,000 — the largest force ever sent to Ireland — against Tyrone. He returned home against orders without fighting a battle.
p3: Tyrone's ultimate defeat by Mountjoy secured Ireland for England. Gaelic lords flee and allow for Protestant plantations in Ulster. England never seriously threatened.

front: What were the specific events of Essex's rise?
p1: Robert Devereux, the Earl of Essex, rose to Elizabeth's court as the godson of Leicester and due to his marriage to the daughter of Francis Walsingham. His wit, eloquence and dashing personality quickly made him a favourite of the ageing Elizabeth in the 1590s.
p2: Essex was raised to the Privy Council in 1593 due to his personality more than his political skills. His flamboyant arrogance often clashed with the more pragmatic Lord Burghley and his son Robert Cecil.
p3: Essex frequently acted unilaterally: in 1589 he joined Drake's English Armada against Elizabeth's direct orders; in 1592 he disobeyed orders to confer with Henry IV of France; his burning of Cadiz in 1596 made him extremely popular across England.

front: What led to Essex's downfall and rebellion?
p1: In the 1590s, Essex was jealous of loss of power. Initially refused to go to Ireland on Elizabeth's orders before being slapped and half drawing his sword.
p2: In Ireland in 1599, Essex led 16,000 men but never fought a battle and returned to London without permission. His defiant return enraged Elizabeth — Essex was placed under house arrest.
p3: Whilst in house arrest Essex lost his monopoly over sweet wines. The success of Lord Mountjoy in crushing the Tyrone Rebellion further disgraced him. In desperation Essex began his 1601 rebellion.

front: What were the key events and consequences of Essex's Rebellion?
p1: Essex wrote to James VI of Scotland that Robert Cecil would prevent his succession. Controversially commissioned performance of banned play Richard II — in which a childless monarch is deposed by a noble.
p2: Essex gathered supporters in the City of London including the Earl of Southampton. He attempted to raise the citizens against Cecil — but most of his supporters got cold feet. The rebellion was quickly defeated as guns of Tower turned on Essex House.
p3: Essex and just 5 supporters were executed in 1601. From then on, Cecil's faction controlled government unopposed — Cecil managed the smooth transition to James I in 1603.

front: What were the specific causes of the 1590s socioeconomic crisis?
p1: A series of bad harvests from 1594–98 led to the average price of wheat doubling. Cheaper grains like oats or rye increased at an even faster rate, affecting the poorest most. At the peak of the crisis in 1595–7 the death rate increased by 50%.
p2: The increasing population continued to outstrip resources — a Malthusian Crisis. Continued influx of bullion from the New World combined with the collapse of trade due to ongoing wars increased prices.
p3: Tax burden: during the War with Spain parliament approved unprecedented levels of taxation in 1589 and 1593. Elizabeth's granting of monopolies to her favourites in the latter years often increased prices on staple goods.

front: How did Elizabeth manage her physical image and public portraiture in her later years?
p1: As Elizabeth entered her 60s, her looks diminished — her fondness for sugar had blackened her teeth; her grey hair was hidden by a bright red wig; her face, pockmarked from Smallpox in 1562, was always heavily made-up with white lead paint.
p2: In her official portraits Elizabeth still appeared as young as in her coronation in 1558. In 1596 the Privy Council ordered the destruction of any 'unseemly and improper' portraits — all portraits had to be based on an agreed, flattering version produced by Nicholas Hilliard.
p3: Portraits like the Rainbow Portrait used heavy symbolism — she holds a rainbow (peace and divine favour); on her dress are eyes and ears (Elizabeth sees and hears all, no one can plot against her).

front: How did Elizabeth manage her reputation at court and among the people in her later years?
p1: A series of scandals undermined Elizabeth's image at court — including Walter Raleigh's disgrace at making Bess Throckmorton (one of Elizabeth's closest ladies) pregnant. Attendance at court tailed off and the nobility were sometimes reluctant to accompany Elizabeth on progress.
p2: However every year on November 17, Accession Day Tilts were lavishly celebrated. Works like Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene glorified Elizabeth as 'Gloriana'. Festivals were encouraged amongst ordinary people on Accession Day to celebrate Elizabeth as England and Protestantism's saviour.
p3: The socioeconomic unrest of the 1590s led to increased criticism — some commented 'We shall never have a merry world while the queen liveth'. Yet her final parliament of 1601, with its famous Golden Speech, was seen as a glorious end to an era.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was communism?
p1: Developed by Marx and Engels in the 19th century — the proletariat (workers) would overthrow capitalism in a socialist revolution and create a classless, equal society.
p2: Lenin adapted Marx's ideas for Russia, founding the Bolshevik Party in 1903 which seized power in October 1917. The USSR became an authoritarian state with no democratic elections and limited freedom of speech.
p3: Marxism-Leninism was opposed to religion ('the opium of the masses'), to private property and to parliamentary democracy, which it dismissed as a camouflage for capitalism.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was capitalism and how did it differ from communism?
p1: Capitalism is an economic system based on private investment and profit — run by people who wish to make a profit, producing what people want rather than by the state.
p2: The West believed in liberty of the individual, equality before the law, freedom of speech and elected government — parliament elected by the people to whom the government is ultimately responsible.
p3: The USSR dismissed parliamentary democracy as a camouflage for capitalism. For Marxist-Leninists, democracy meant economic equality under the dictatorship of the proletariat — not political freedom.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: Why were there long-term tensions between the USSR and the West before 1941?
p1: The Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 alarmed Western powers — Britain, USA, France and Japan all intervened in Russia's Civil War (1917–22) on the side of the Whites against the communists.
p2: The Comintern (1919) confirmed Western fears the USSR sought to export revolution. The 1920s and 1930s saw a Red Scare in the USA. Stalin's show trials reinforced Western perceptions of a brutal dictatorship.
p3: The Nazi-Soviet Pact of 1939 shocked the West — confirming communism and fascism had more in common than communism and democracy. The 1938 Munich Agreement had convinced Stalin the West wanted Germany and Russia to fight each other.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was the Atlantic Charter and why was it significant?
p1: A joint British and American document signed in August 1941, affirming war aims including self-determination, political freedom and freedom of speech — directly threatening Soviet ideas.
p2: The USSR 'endorsed' it alongside 125 other nations in January 1942, but was not part of writing it. Stalin resented being presented with Western values as a condition of alliance.
p3: It demonstrated the fundamental incompatibility of Western and Soviet war aims — the West was fighting for liberal democracy while the USSR sought a buffer zone of compliant states. This tension would resurface at every wartime conference.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was the second front dispute and why did it cause tension?
p1: The USSR proposed that the Allies create a Second Front through France — Stalin felt he had been fighting the bulk of the war in Europe alone while the Western Allies defended their territories in North Africa.
p2: Britain and the USA stalled on opening the Second Front until June 1944 — Churchill wanted it opened in the Balkans to prevent Soviet influence there. Stalin believed the delay was deliberate to weaken the USSR.
p3: Soviet foreign minister Andrei Gromyko argued that 'the Cold War began as a secret Cold War when the Allies delayed the opening of the second front in Europe.' The delay deepened Stalin's suspicion of Western intentions.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: Why was Poland such a divisive issue in the Grand Alliance?
p1: The West had gone to war to defend Polish independence — Britain was hosting the Polish government in exile and had recognised them as legitimate. Abandoning Poland would be seen as a betrayal.
p2: The USSR saw Poland as a vital buffer zone — it had been invaded via Poland three times and had already seized eastern Polish territory in the Nazi-Soviet Pact. Stalin wanted a 'friendly' (i.e. communist) Polish government.
p3: Poland symbolised the fundamental clash of war aims — the West wanted self-determination and free elections; the USSR wanted security through compliant neighbours. The dispute over Poland at Yalta and Potsdam set the pattern for the Cold War division of Europe.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was the Percentages Agreement (1944)?
p1: In October 1944, Churchill visited Moscow and brokered a secret deal with Stalin dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence — Romania 90% Soviet, Greece 90% British, Hungary and Yugoslavia 50/50.
p2: Churchill scribbled the percentages on a piece of paper and pushed it across to Stalin — who ticked it. Churchill described it as a 'naughty document'.
p3: It showed the contempt both leaders had for the wishes of Eastern Europeans. This was never put into practice as the USA would not have agreed — but it revealed that Churchill and Stalin were already dividing Europe between them, undermining later Western claims to be fighting for self-determination.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was agreed at the Tehran Conference (1943)?
p1: The 'Big Three' (Stalin, Roosevelt, Churchill) met for the first time. Main aims were to direct wartime strategy.
p2: The USA and UK promised to open a second front — D-Day would take place in May/June 1944. Stalin agreed to declare war on Japan once Germany was defeated.
p3: There was a vague agreement Germany would remain weak after the war. It was the most cooperative of the three wartime conferences — the common enemy still dominated and attention had not yet turned to the post-war world.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was agreed at the Yalta Conference (February 1945)?
p1: Germany would be split into four occupation zones; Berlin also split into four; Germany to pay $20 billion in reparations (half to USSR); UN to be established.
p2: Stalin promised free elections in Eastern Europe. Eastern Europe would be a Soviet 'sphere of influence' — though this was never clearly defined. Stalin wanted greater UN representation for individual Soviet republics.
p3: Poland was disagreed: Stalin wanted the communist Lublin Committee; Britain had hosted the Polish government in exile. There was little to guarantee Stalin would deliver free elections — the vague language of Yalta contained the seeds of future conflict.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was disagreed at the Potsdam Conference (July–August 1945)?
p1: Britain and America did not want harsh reparations on Germany — they feared a repeat of Versailles and wanted Germany to recover as a buffer against communism. Stalin, who had lost 25 million people, wanted very harsh reparations.
p2: Truman strongly objected to the Soviet presence in Eastern Europe and the lack of free elections — between Yalta and Potsdam, Stalin had installed a communist puppet government in Poland, breaking his promise.
p3: Truman informed Stalin of the atomic bomb vaguely during the conference. The bombs were dropped on Hiroshima (6 August) and Nagasaki (9 August) without telling Stalin — he saw this as a direct threat. No general peace settlement was reached.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: How did the liberation of Europe differ between East and West?
p1: Western liberation: in France, the Low Countries and Denmark, Allied forces were seen as liberators — bringing supplies with no thought of annexing territory or imposing an ideology.
p2: Eastern liberation: the Red Army inflicted harsh retribution — terrible reprisals against civilians, widespread plunder, deportation of ethnic Germans. Pre-1918 Russian territories were restored to Soviet control by annexation.
p3: Soviet political influence spread rapidly — they supported communist coups in Romania (1945), installed communist-dominated coalitions in Hungary and Bulgaria and established pro-Soviet committees in Poland. By 1948, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia had been absorbed into the USSR.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the United Nations and how did it immediately become a Cold War battleground?
p1: The UN was established on 24 October 1945, replacing the ineffective League of Nations. The Security Council gave five permanent members (USA, USSR, UK, France and China) the power of veto.
p2: At its very first meeting in 1946, Russia used the first Security Council veto to block a plan for Britain and France to withdraw from Syria and Lebanon. The Atomic Control Commission was created — but the USA proposed international control of atomic weapons; the USSR rejected this.
p3: Despite Cold War tensions, the UN provided a forum for diplomacy that helped prevent direct superpower conflict. It played a key role in the Korean War (1950–53) when the USSR was boycotting the Security Council and the USA secured a resolution authorising military action.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What did Churchill say in his Iron Curtain speech (March 1946)?
p1: 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the continent.' The speech was made in Fulton, Missouri, and was called 'The Sinews of Peace'.
p2: Churchill argued the USSR wanted to expand without limit; the West needed to negotiate from a position of strength — 'supported by the whole strength of the English-speaking world'. He saw Stalin as admiring strength and despising weakness.
p3: Stalin reacted by accusing Churchill of being 'a firebrand of war'. Many in the USA thought the speech irresponsible. Despite its inaccuracies (Soviet influence was not yet uniform across Eastern Europe), the speech gave voice to Western fears of Soviet expansionism and helped harden attitudes on both sides.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What were salami tactics?
p1: The USSR's method of taking control of Eastern European governments — entering into coalition governments with other parties, then when the time was right 'slicing them out' of the coalition.
p2: Methods included: carefully controlled elections using violence and intimidation; forced mergers between socialist parties and communists; extensive propaganda; establishment of political police; arrests and murder of opposition leaders.
p3: By 1948, unrepresentative pro-Moscow communist leaders had been established across Eastern Europe and all opposition had been destroyed. The term was coined by Hungarian communist leader Mátyás Rákosi.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: How did the USSR take control of Poland?
p1: Soviet forces set up a Provisional Government in June 1945 dominated by Polish communists who had little support in the country. When the London Poles (government in exile) joined, it was obvious there would be no free elections.
p2: The non-communist Peasant Party representatives resigned in protest. By 1947 the communist-dominated government had repressed all opposition.
p3: Poland was the most symbolically important case — Britain had gone to war to defend Polish independence. The failure to deliver free elections was the clearest early breach of the Yalta agreements and confirmed Western fears about Soviet intentions.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: How did the USSR take control of Czechoslovakia?
p1: Elections in March 1946 gave Czech communists 38% of the vote — genuinely free. By 1947 there was more pressure for communist domination. The USSR was determined to prevent the Czechs accepting Marshall Aid.
p2: In February 1948 a communist coup took place — the police force was taken over by communists; non-communist personnel were purged; non-communist ministers were removed from government. Foreign minister Jan Masaryk was thrown from a window, probably by the security police. President Benes was forced to resign.
p3: The Czech coup had important psychological significance for the West — it played on feelings of guilt (Britain had failed to prevent Hitler taking Czechoslovakia in 1938–9) and accelerated the formation of NATO.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the Long Telegram and the Novikov Telegram?
p1: Long Telegram (February 1946): George Kennan, the US ambassador in Moscow, sent an 8,000-word report to Truman arguing Stalin was planning the destruction of capitalism and world communism. Kennan also argued Stalin was not suicidal — faced with enough pressure he would back down.
p2: Novikov Telegram (September 1946): Soviet ambassador Novikov in Washington reported that the US were planning to use their new military might to dominate the world and that, since Roosevelt's death, cooperation was impossible.
p3: Both telegrams confirmed to each side that the other was their enemy — they increased the paranoia on both sides and shaped the foreign policies of Truman and Stalin. The Long Telegram became the intellectual basis for the policy of containment.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the Truman Doctrine?
p1: On 12 March 1947, Truman appealed to Congress to strengthen non-communist forces in areas thought vulnerable to communist domination — committing the USA to an active foreign policy of containment.
p2: He set out two competing ways of life: one based on free institutions, representative government and individual liberty; the other based on terror, oppression and the will of a minority. He pledged $400 million to Greece and Turkey.
p3: The trigger was Britain's inability to keep financing anti-communist fighters in Greece. By 1947 Stalin was not keeping to his Yalta agreements about elections in Eastern Europe. The Doctrine ended American isolationism and committed the USA to opposing communism globally.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the Marshall Plan?
p1: In June 1947, Secretary of State George Marshall offered an aid package of $13 billion to Europe. No distinction was made between 'free' and 'unfree' countries — but Stalin forbade Soviet-dominated nations to attend the Paris meeting.
p2: 16 nations attended without the Soviet bloc. Congress approved the policy in 1948. Most of the $12.7 billion in aid was used to purchase US goods and raw materials. It supported the re-industrialisation of West Germany and promoted political stability.
p3: Stalin labelled it 'Dollar Imperialism' — turning Europe into an American economic empire. It forced Stalin to consolidate his hold on Eastern Europe — creating Cominform (1947) and Comecon (1949). Europe was now divided into two competing economic camps.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
