front: What was Cominform?
p1: The Communist Information Bureau (September 1947): Stalin banned Soviet bloc governments from accepting Marshall Aid and created Cominform to coordinate all European communist parties.
p2: Its aims were to 'provide information to strengthen the anti-imperialist democratic camp' — in practice it was propaganda to prevent any communist party being lured by US 'dollar diplomacy' and to maintain Soviet ideological control.
p3: The most significant consequence was the expulsion of Yugoslavia — Tito resisted Stalin's control, wanted to apply for Marshall Aid and refused subordination to Moscow. Yugoslavia was expelled in 1948, showing the limits of Soviet control. Cominform was abolished in 1956.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was Comecon?
p1: The Council of Mutual Economic Assistance (1949): created as an economic alliance parallel to the Marshall Plan. Initial members were the USSR, Albania, Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Poland and Czechoslovakia.
p2: During the Stalin era there was direct economic aid to Eastern Europe, but Comecon did not develop much in the way of regional cooperation — economic life was dominated by relations between Comecon members and the USSR, providing an outlet for Soviet manufacturers and raw materials.
p3: Comecon helped divide Europe into two competing economic blocs and boosted the USSR's control of its satellites. Unlike the Marshall Plan it did not provide an engine for growth — it kept Eastern economies subordinate to Soviet interests.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What caused the Berlin Blockade?
p1: Germany was divided into four occupation zones. The West wanted Germany to recover as a buffer; the USSR wanted reparations and a weak Germany. In January 1947 Bizonia was created from the US and British zones.
p2: In June 1948 the West introduced the Deutschmark for West Germany without consulting the USSR — Stalin's key aim was to prevent the creation of a West German state. He chose to put pressure on the West's weakest point — West Berlin.
p3: On 23 June 1948 Stalin imposed a blockade on all road and rail links to West Berlin and cut off its electricity. He could not shoot down Allied supply planes without starting a war — so the Allies supplied the city entirely by air.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What happened during the Berlin Airlift and what were its consequences?
p1: Each day 2,000 tonnes of supplies were flown in, reaching 8,000 tonnes a day by February 1949. 60 B29 bombers were stationed in England as a threat. The blockade and airlift ended in May 1949.
p2: The blockade was a propaganda disaster for the USSR — confirming the view of Soviet aggression. It directly accelerated the formation of NATO in April 1949 and led to the creation of two separate German states.
p3: The West's willingness to risk confrontation to defend West Berlin showed the USSR that containment was serious. The airlift became a symbol of Western resolve — and of the West Berlin population's refusal to submit to Soviet pressure.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the East German Rising of 1953?
p1: By 1953 the DDR was in serious difficulty — Ulbricht had imposed harsh economic policies including high production quotas and low wages. On 16–17 June 1953, workers in East Berlin went on strike; protests spread to over 400 towns and cities — around 400,000 people participated.
p2: Demands quickly became political: free elections and the end of the SED regime. Soviet tanks were deployed on 17 June. Around 55 people were killed, 20 were executed and thousands arrested. The uprising was crushed within days.
p3: The East German Rising showed how shallow the roots of communism were in the DDR — workers were rising against a workers' state. In West Germany, 17 June became a national holiday — 'Tag der Deutschen Einheit' — until German reunification in 1990.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was NATO and why was it created?
p1: The North Atlantic Treaty (4 April 1949): expanding the Brussels Pact after the Berlin Blockade and Czech coup, secret talks between Britain, Canada and the USA created NATO. It promised consultation on mutual interest and assistance in the event of attack.
p2: It had an ideological element — defending not merely national security but 'freedom, common heritage and civilisation'. NATO was like a wartime alliance but with distinct political aims.
p3: NATO expansion was driven by events: in September 1949 the USSR tested its first atomic bomb; in 1950 North Korea invaded South Korea; in 1952 a permanent HQ was established in Paris with a permanent military force of 35 divisions. West Germany joined NATO in May 1955.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the Warsaw Pact and why was it created?
p1: Signed on 14 May 1955 by the USSR and most Eastern European satellites (the DDR signed in 1956). It promised consultation on mutual interest and assistance in the event of an attack on any one member country.
p2: Unlike NATO, it was not an agreement between independent states — it was a policy move by the USSR in direct response to West Germany joining NATO. If 'a general European treaty of Collective Security' were signed it would lapse — indicating it was more political than defensive.
p3: Though it seemed to divide Europe into armed camps, little had actually changed — Moscow already controlled the foreign and defence policies of its allies. But it meant suppression of discontent would now be by 'the Warsaw Pact' rather than the USSR alone — a convenient fiction.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: How did the arms race develop between 1945 and 1955?
p1: USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, ending WWII. Stalin immediately accelerated the Soviet nuclear programme. The USSR tested its first atomic bomb in 1949 — years earlier than the West expected. In 1952 the USA tested the hydrogen bomb — vastly more destructive; the USSR tested its own in 1953.
p2: The USA shifted strategic policy to 'mutually assured destruction' (MAD) — any Russian attack would lead to devastating retaliatory strikes with the capacity to destroy half the Russian population and 80% of its industry.
p3: The arms race perpetuated the Cold War but prevented it developing into a direct conflict — neither side could win a nuclear war. It drove the economic overstretch that would eventually contribute to the USSR's collapse in 1991.

front: What was Khrushchev's secret speech (1956)?
p1: In February 1956 Khrushchev gave his 'secret speech' at the 20th Party Congress, denouncing Stalin's crimes — the purges, show trials, cult of personality and abuse of power.
p2: The speech raised hopes of liberalisation across Eastern Europe where communist regimes had shallow roots. It was called the beginning of 'de-Stalinisation' — a thaw in the oppressive policies of the Stalin era.
p3: The speech had unintended consequences — it unleashed expectations for reform that Khrushchev could not fully satisfy. It directly contributed to the Polish October and Hungarian Uprising of 1956, as people across Eastern Europe took the speech as a signal that change was possible.

front: What was the Polish October (1956)?
p1: In Poland, protests began in June 1956 at the Poznan factories — initially demanding better wages but quickly becoming political. The party itself was divided; the liberal wing asserted itself and refused to accept Russia's nominee as defence minister.
p2: In October 1956, party support went to Wladyslaw Gomulka — a communist who had been imprisoned from 1949 to 1954 for 'deviationist' activities. Support for Gomulka grew in the so-called 'Polish October'. Khrushchev accepted Gomulka rather than launching a massive invasion.
p3: Gomulka proved to be a limited reformer — loyal to the USSR and to the Warsaw Pact. The unrest in Poland was a major factor in similar, more serious unrest in Hungary. The Polish October showed Khrushchev would accept limited reform to avoid a full rebellion.

front: What caused the Hungarian Uprising of 1956?
p1: Hungary resented Stalinist policies — Rakosi's brutal rule, the AVH secret police, collectivisation and Soviet economic controls. Khrushchev's secret speech raised hopes for reform.
p2: On 23 October 1956 police fired on protesters, leading to workers joining students and intellectuals in protest. Imre Nagy — a previously disgraced liberal communist — took power, releasing political prisoners, ending the one-party state and asking Khrushchev to remove Soviet troops. Khrushchev initially accepted.
p3: However Nagy went too far — announcing Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact and become a neutral non-aligned country. This could cause a chain reaction across the Eastern bloc — Khrushchev ordered the invasion.

front: What happened during the Hungarian Uprising and what were its consequences?
p1: Khrushchev ordered the invasion — over 1,000 tanks rolled into Budapest. 3,000 Hungarians were killed; 180,000 fled to the West. Janos Kadar was installed as a loyal but eventually pragmatic leader. Nagy was executed in 1958.
p2: The West failed to help — distracted by the Suez Crisis. The USA disapproved of the British and French invasion of Suez, meaning the West was divided at a crucial time. This showed that America would not intervene to defend the satellite states.
p3: Consequences: the failure of the USA to intervene revealed the limitations of containment. There was little long-term interruption of contacts between East and West. The West had accepted that Hungary was part of the Soviet bloc — NATO was a defensive alliance and the iron curtain was a reality.

front: Why did West Germany rearm and join NATO (1955)?
p1: The Korean War (1950–53) showed NATO needed more ground forces in Europe. A European Defence Community (EDC) was proposed in 1950 but France rejected it in 1954, fearing German dominance of a European force.
p2: A compromise was reached: in October 1954 France agreed to a limited West German army. Germany was not to have nuclear weapons and British forces would remain in Germany as a safeguard. West Germany joined NATO in May 1955.
p3: The Warsaw Pact was signed just days after West Germany joined NATO — in direct response. West German rearmament increased East German fears and accelerated the brain drain — by 1961, 3.5 million East Germans had fled West, creating the crisis that led to the Berlin Wall.

front: What caused the brain drain and Khrushchev's Berlin Ultimatum?
p1: The division of Germany produced a relatively open frontier — people could move between East and West Berlin without checks. By 1961 3.5 million East Germans had fled West — 20% of the population, including the best educated and trained.
p2: In July and early August 1961 alone, 36,000 left via Berlin. Khrushchev needed to show the world that Soviet economic policies worked — but in East Germany they were obviously failing. He had also issued the Berlin Ultimatum in 1958 (demanding the West leave West Berlin within 6 months) with no result.
p3: The Paris summit (1960) between Khrushchev and Eisenhower failed when a US U-2 spy plane was shot down over the USSR — Eisenhower refused to apologise for spying so Khrushchev stormed out. By 1961 the crisis demanded a permanent solution.

front: Why was the Berlin Wall built and what was its significance?
p1: On 12–13 August 1961 barriers were erected and the Wall was built on 17 August. A second inner wall was constructed in 1962 with a 'zone of death' between. Some 5,000 managed to escape up to 1989; there were possibly 136 deaths among those attempting to escape.
p2: Kennedy increased troop numbers and made his famous Berlin speech in June 1963: 'Ich bin ein Berliner'. US Secretary of State Dean Rusk called the Wall 'a monument to communist failure' — its purpose was to keep East Germans from defecting, not to separate East from West.
p3: The Wall confirmed the status quo in Europe and ended hopes that détente might lead to fundamental change. It showed communist leaders were now wedded to defence of a failing system. Its fall on 9 November 1989 became the defining symbol of the Cold War's end.

front: What caused the Cuban Missile Crisis?
p1: Cuba became communist under Castro in 1959. The USA sponsored the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961. Khrushchev placed nuclear missiles in Cuba to defend it and to counter US Jupiter missiles in Turkey, which were a direct threat to the USSR.
p2: In October 1962 a U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet missile installations in Cuba. Kennedy chose a naval blockade ('quarantine') rather than an air strike and demanded the missiles be removed.
p3: For 13 days the world held its breath as Soviet ships carrying missiles approached the US quarantine line. Soviet submarines were in the area. The crisis brought both sides closer to nuclear war than any other Cold War event.

front: How was the Cuban Missile Crisis resolved and what were its consequences?
p1: Khrushchev offered to remove the missiles if the USA pledged not to invade Cuba. Kennedy publicly accepted this and secretly agreed to remove the Jupiter missiles from Turkey. Khrushchev was seen to have backed down first.
p2: Consequences for Khrushchev: America had been forced to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey; Cuba remained communist. However Khrushchev was humiliated and was ousted in 1964, replaced by Brezhnev.
p3: Consequences for both sides: 1963 — nuclear hotline established; 1963 — Limited Test Ban Treaty; 1968 — Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The crisis made both sides more determined to avoid future nuclear confrontations — and became a key reason for détente.

front: What was the Space Race and what were the key events?
p1: Sputnik (October 1957): the USSR launched the first man-made satellite — shocking the USA and showing Soviet technology was no longer lagging behind. Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space (April 1961). First woman in space: Valentina Tereshkova (June 1963). First spacewalk: Alexei Leonov (March 1965).
p2: US response: NASA was formed using German scientist Werner von Braun's rocket knowledge. Kennedy pledged in September 1962 to put a man on the moon by the end of the decade. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the moon on 20 July 1969.
p3: The Space Race mattered as a direct Cold War competition for technological and ideological prestige. Soviet early successes challenged assumptions of Western superiority. The first joint US-Soviet space mission — Apollo-Soyuz (1975) — symbolised the spirit of détente.

front: What was the Prague Spring (1968)?
p1: In January 1968, Alexander Dubček became leader of the Czech Communist Party and launched the 'Prague Spring' — liberalisation including freedom of speech and press, multi-party democracy, and 'socialism with a human face'.
p2: The USSR was alarmed — if the Czechs could liberalise, other satellite states would follow. Brezhnev warned Dubček repeatedly but he refused to abandon his reforms.
p3: In August 1968 the USSR, Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria and East Germany invaded Czechoslovakia with 500,000 troops. Dubček was taken to Moscow and 'encouraged' to abandon his reforms. 150 Czechoslovak civilians were killed. Jan Palach set himself on fire in protest. Hard-line Gustáv Husák replaced Dubček.

front: What were the consequences of the Czech Crisis of 1968?
p1: America failed to help — too distracted by Vietnam, again showing the West would not intervene in the Soviet sphere. Albania left the Warsaw Pact in protest. Yugoslavia and Romania condemned the invasion and began to foster closer links with China. Western communist parties cut ties with the USSR.
p2: Brezhnev issued the Brezhnev Doctrine to justify the invasion — if any communist country was showing signs of turning towards capitalism, it was the responsibility of all communist countries to force it back to communism.
p3: The doctrine cast a long shadow over Eastern Europe, making clear to reformers in Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia that there were firm limits to change. Gorbachev replaced it with the 'Sinatra Doctrine' in 1988 — this was the key decision enabling the 1989 revolutions.

front: What was the Brezhnev Doctrine?
p1: Issued after the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968: if any communist country showed signs of turning towards capitalism, it was the responsibility of all communist countries to force it back to communism.
p2: It asserted 'limited sovereignty' — communist states were not fully sovereign if their actions threatened the socialist bloc as a whole. This directly contradicted the UN Charter's principle of national self-determination.
p3: In practice, it meant any satellite state attempting to leave the Warsaw Pact or adopt multi-party democracy would face Soviet military intervention. Gorbachev replaced it with the 'Sinatra Doctrine' in 1988 — satellite states were free to 'do it their way' — enabling the 1989 revolutions.

front: What was Solidarity and why was it significant?
p1: Economic unrest — strikes in the Gdansk shipyards in 1980 — led the Polish government to recognise Solidarity, the first independent trade union in the Eastern bloc, led by Lech Walesa.
p2: In April 1981 Round Table Agreements saw Solidarity recognised as a political party. General Jaruzelski declared martial law in December 1981, suspending Solidarity and arresting Walesa. However the elections of June 1989 resulted in a Solidarity government — the first non-communist government in Eastern Europe since 1948.
p3: Solidarity was the first mass movement to successfully challenge Soviet-bloc communist authority without being crushed by tanks. The role of Pope John Paul II — a Pole elected in 1979 — was crucial in strengthening the resolve of the Polish people.

front: What was détente and why did it develop?
p1: Détente (1969–1979) was a period of improved superpower relations. Reasons: the USSR faced worsening relations with China and serious border clashes in 1969; the USA faced the costly Vietnam War and oil price rises in 1973; both sides recognised arms reduction would help their economies.
p2: Both sides had been frightened by how close they had come to nuclear war in Cuba in 1962. By the 1970s, more pragmatic leaders — Brezhnev in the USSR and Nixon (advised by Kissinger) in the USA — based policy on national interest rather than ideology.
p3: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (Christmas Day 1979) ended détente and began the new Cold War. SALT II was proposed but never ratified — cancelled by Carter after Afghanistan. The Olympic boycotts (1980 and 1984) symbolised the collapse of détente.

front: What was SALT I?
p1: Strategic Arms Limitation Talks: established a 5-year freeze on constructing missile launchers and a freeze on ICBMs and submarine-launched ballistic missiles. Both sides agreed to restrict anti-ballistic screens to their capital cities and main missile sites.
p2: Both sides still had enough nuclear weapons to initiate MAD — but it symbolised improving relations. Nixon and Brezhnev visited each other in 1972/3.
p3: SALT I was significant as the first formal arms limitation agreement between the superpowers — showing both sides recognised the dangers of the arms race. It laid the groundwork for SALT II (1979) and the Helsinki Accords (1975).

front: What were the Helsinki Accords (1975)?
p1: 33 nations from NATO and the Warsaw Pact met at the Helsinki Conference. Three 'baskets' were agreed: Basket 1 — European borders are inviolable; Basket 2 — economic and scientific co-operation; Basket 3 — human rights are to be respected.
p2: Later that year Basket 2's vision was followed up by the Apollo-Soyuz Mission — the first joint US-Soviet space mission. This was seen as the zenith of détente.
p3: In practice the Helsinki Accords were 'just a piece of paper' — the human rights provisions of Basket 3 were regularly ignored by the USSR. However, Basket 3 gave Eastern European dissidents a legal basis to demand their rights, and this became increasingly important in the 1980s.

front: What was Ostpolitik?
p1: Ostpolitik ('East Politics') was pursued by West German Chancellor Willy Brandt from 1969. The FRG Hallstein Doctrine had stated West Germany would break off relations with any state recognising the DDR — Brandt abandoned this.
p2: Key treaties: Moscow Treaty (August 1970) — neither Germany had territorial claims against any other state; western frontier of Poland recognised; Germany accepted the loss of 1945 territory as 'inviolable'. Basic Treaty (December 1972) — FRG recognised the DDR as an equal sovereign state; both Germanies became UN members.
p3: Brandt won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971. Ostpolitik gained concessions for West Berlin and did not weaken ties with the USA or NATO. The way was left open for future reunification — achieved in 1990. It showed that patient diplomacy could produce real gains without military confrontation.

front: Why did the USSR invade Afghanistan (1979)?
p1: In 1978 a communist party (PDPA) seized power in Afghanistan. Many Afghans rejected the communist government — its atheism conflicted with their Muslim faith; the communists imprisoned and murdered Muslim religious leaders. An anti-communist resistance movement (the Mujahedeen) formed.
p2: Brezhnev invaded on Christmas Day 1979 with 100,000 Soviet forces to support the communist government. They faced guerrilla opposition inspired by Islamic beliefs and supplied by the USA via Pakistan.
p3: The invasion ended détente and triggered the new Cold War. Carter cancelled SALT II, ended the grain trade with the USSR and issued the Carter Doctrine — stating that America would respond strongly to any attempts to take control of the Persian Gulf.

front: What were the consequences of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan?
p1: The terrain led to a sustained guerrilla war echoing the US struggle in Vietnam. The opposition fighters had the support of local populations. Soviet troops withdrew in 1989 after 10 years — over 38,000 Soviets died or were wounded.
p2: The war eroded the confidence of Soviet leaders in using military intervention — this directly influenced Gorbachev's decision not to use force to maintain communist regimes in 1989. It weakened the Red Army's reputation.
p3: The losses increased resentment within the USSR from non-Russians. When glasnost allowed press freedom, the reporting of the war brought about discontent and demand for political change. The spiralling costs of the war were another drain on a Russian economy already struggling to meet heavier defence demands.

front: What was the new Cold War (1979–1984)?
p1: Reagan took office in January 1981 describing the USSR as an 'evil empire'. He dramatically increased US military spending — from $171 billion in 1981 to $376 billion by 1986. He developed the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI — 'Star Wars'): a space-based laser system to intercept Soviet ICBMs, threatening to make all Soviet nuclear missiles obsolete.
p2: Reagan stationed Pershing and Cruise missiles in Western Europe in 1983. America boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics; the USSR boycotted the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics. In 1983 the USSR shot down South Korean airliner KAL 007 — killing all 269 people, intensifying mutual hostility.
p3: Soviet military spending was already high and did not dramatically increase in response to Reagan's build-up — it was internal economic stagnation that forced Gorbachev to seek arms reduction. Reagan's SDI was nevertheless crucial in bringing Gorbachev to the negotiating table.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What problems was the USSR facing in the 1980s?
p1: Brezhnev's 'era of stagnation' — the Soviet economy was failing. The war in Afghanistan cost vast amounts with no results — over 38,000 Soviets died or were wounded. In 1986 the Chernobyl nuclear power station exploded — $18 billion spent on containment, exposing the inefficiency and corruption of Soviet industry.
p2: Poor living standards and lack of human rights caused unrest in satellite states — for example Solidarity in Poland. Reagan's SDI threatened to make all Soviet ICBMs obsolete. The two elderly leaders who followed Brezhnev — Andropov and Chernenko — meant stagnation characterised policy at a vital time.
p3: When Gorbachev became leader in 1985 at 54 — relatively young — there was widespread understanding that severe economic problems existed and radical change was needed. The Soviet economy was over-spending on defence, producing insufficient consumer goods and losing the technological race with the West.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What was perestroika?
p1: Perestroika ('restructuring'): relaxed centralised control and permitted greater economic freedom and initiative. In June 1987 private enterprise was allowed in some industries. The Soviet state retained control of key industries.
p2: However the changes did not lead to grateful appreciation — new private industries were not all efficient, long-term economic problems continued and there were more shortages of some goods than before. The disruption to economic life caused job losses and uncertainty.
p3: Perestroika was intended to save the communist system — but by opening the economy to market forces, it unleashed expectations and inequalities the system could not manage. Combined with glasnost, it set in motion forces that would ultimately destroy the USSR.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What was glasnost?
p1: Glasnost ('openness'): in 1986 state controls of the media were relaxed and the public learnt about the inefficiencies and corruption in national and local government. Greater freedom of speech and the press — political prisoners were released.
p2: In January 1987 Gorbachev proposed multi-candidate elections by secret ballot for local councils. In February 1989 elections for a new Congress of People's Deputies saw the defeat of many party establishment figures — new leaders emerged, including Boris Yeltsin.
p3: Glasnost was intended to drive progress through open discussion — but it revealed how deep the problems were. When glasnost allowed press freedom, the reporting of the Afghanistan war and Chernobyl brought about discontent and demand for political change that Gorbachev could not control.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What was the Sinatra Doctrine?
p1: In 1988 Gorbachev replaced the Brezhnev Doctrine with the 'Sinatra Doctrine' — satellite states were now free to 'do it their way'. This was aimed at easing Soviet military spending and avoiding hypocrisy.
p2: The Sinatra Doctrine was the single most important decision enabling the 1989 revolutions — it removed the threat of Soviet military intervention that had crushed the Hungarian Uprising (1956) and Czech Crisis (1968).
p3: By 1989, Gorbachev would not bolster unpopular communist regimes that were unwilling to apply the remedies he had introduced in the USSR. The contrast with the Brezhnev Doctrine was stark — and the satellite states moved rapidly to exploit the new freedom.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: How did Reagan and Gorbachev work together to reduce tensions?
p1: At Reykjavik (1986) Gorbachev attempted to persuade Reagan to give up SDI — he failed, but he succeeded in securing the INF Treaty (Washington, 1987): the total withdrawal of medium-range missiles from Europe. This was the first arms reduction (not just limitation) agreement of the Cold War.
p2: Gorbachev stopped increasing SS-20 missiles stationed in Eastern Europe in April 1985. Reagan and Gorbachev visited each other's countries and developed a working relationship — Reagan came to believe Gorbachev was genuinely different from previous Soviet leaders.
p3: The new détente of 1985–88 was an indication that the USSR was susceptible to pressure. But the primary driver was Gorbachev's realisation that the USSR needed to reduce military spending to save its economy — Western pressure was a contributory factor, not the primary cause.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What happened in Poland in 1989?
p1: Economic unrest including strikes in the shipyards of Gdansk led the government to recognise Solidarity once more. In April 1989 Round Table Agreements saw Solidarity recognised as a political party, allowed to compete with the Communist Party for 35% of parliamentary seats.
p2: The elections of June 1989 resulted in a Solidarity government — the first non-communist government in Eastern Europe since 1948. The existing leader Jaruzelski remained president and Communists held key posts in the new government.
p3: Poland remained part of the Warsaw Pact but the USSR had accepted a non-Communist government and important constitutional change. Poland's revolution showed that the Sinatra Doctrine was real — and triggered a wave of revolutions across Eastern Europe.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What happened in Hungary in 1989?
p1: Unrest in 1988 resulted in the replacement of Kadar by a reforming communist, Grosz, who planned to introduce a multi-party system in 1989. It was agreed to hold free elections in 1990.
p2: Hungary opened its borders with Austria in August 1989 — this made it possible for 150,000 East Germans to leave for the West via this route. This triggered the crisis that led to the fall of the Berlin Wall.
p3: Hungary's peaceful transition showed that communism could be reformed away without violence — in sharp contrast to Romania. It also played a crucial indirect role in bringing about German reunification by enabling the mass exodus of East Germans that made the Berlin Wall untenable.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What was the Velvet Revolution in Czechoslovakia (1989)?
p1: News from Berlin led to large-scale demonstrations for political change in Czechoslovakia. Opposition groups including Charter 77, led by the dramatist Vaclav Havel, formed Civic Forum and demanded change.
p2: The Communist Party relinquished power and a coalition government was formed in December in which Communists were only a minority. Havel was made president. The so-called 'Velvet Revolution' — named for its peaceful nature.
p3: The Velvet Revolution led to the end of communism and the formation of two states — Slovakia and the Czech Republic — in 1992. It was perhaps the most complete and peaceful of the 1989 revolutions, demonstrating that decades of communist rule had failed to eliminate democratic political culture.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What happened in Romania in 1989?
p1: Romania was the only violent revolution of 1989. Demonstrations against President Ceausescu began in the city of Timisoara in November 1989, influenced by events in Hungary, and then spread.
p2: Ceausescu and his wife fled but were captured and executed on 25 December 1989 — the only Eastern European leaders to suffer this fate. Opposition groups formed a coalition and a new leader, Ion Iliescu, was elected.
p3: Romania's violent revolution contrasted with the peaceful transitions elsewhere. It reflected Ceausescu's particularly brutal and personal dictatorship — unlike Gorbachev-aligned reformers elsewhere, he showed no willingness to compromise. The execution of Ceausescu removed any prospect of a negotiated transition.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: Why did the Berlin Wall fall on 9 November 1989?
p1: Hungary's decision to open its borders with Austria allowed 150,000 East Germans to leave for the West, triggering demonstrations in East German cities — especially Leipzig in September and October 1989. The East German leader Honecker could not count on Soviet support — Gorbachev advised him to make changes.
p2: On 9 November 1989 the government announced that East Germans would be allowed to travel freely. As soon as this was announced, border guards — overwhelmed by crowds — opened up crossing points. Crowds began demolishing the Wall with hammers and pickaxes.
p3: The fall of the Wall was the defining symbolic moment of the Cold War's end. Kennedy had pledged in 1963 'Ich bin ein Berliner' — 26 years later the Wall was gone. Its fall confirmed that the Sinatra Doctrine was real and that the Cold War was over.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: How and why was Germany reunified?
p1: West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl moved rapidly to push for reunification, fearing a window of opportunity might close. In March 1990 the first free elections in East Germany were held — the pro-reunification Alliance for Germany won a clear majority.
p2: On 1 July 1990 the economies of the two Germanies merged — the Deutschmark replaced the East German Mark at a 1:1 exchange rate. On 3 October 1990 Germany was formally reunified. The 'Two Plus Four Treaty' with the four wartime Allies formally recognised reunification and settled the borders of the new state.
p3: Reunification brought massive challenges: East German industry was uncompetitive; property rights were confused (over 2 million claims filed); high unemployment in the East; enormous West German investment was needed. Gorbachev agreed in return for assurances NATO would not expand eastwards — an assurance that became highly controversial in later decades.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What caused the coup of August 1991?
p1: Gorbachev's reforms had unleashed forces he could not control. The constituent republics of the USSR saw how easily the satellite states had gained independence and began to demand the same. In 1990, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania declared independence from the USSR.
p2: Gorbachev was increasingly unpopular in Moscow amongst hard-line Communists who felt his reforms had gone too far. In August 1991 eight communist hardliners organised a coup and removed Gorbachev from power — suspending glasnost and perestroika.
p3: However Boris Yeltsin led the resistance — standing on a tank outside the Russian Parliament, he rallied popular opposition. The coup collapsed after just 3 days, restoring Gorbachev to power. The affair demonstrated how little power Gorbachev had now — Yeltsin acted like he was in control.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What were the consequences of the 1991 coup and the collapse of the USSR?
p1: Christmas Day 1991: to avoid a civil war, Gorbachev resigned and announced the breakup of the USSR. The Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin and replaced by the Russian flag. Yeltsin became the 1st president of Russia — turning it capitalist.
p2: The 15 former Soviet republics became independent states. Russia inherited the USSR's permanent seat on the UN Security Council and its nuclear arsenal. The USA emerged as the world's sole superpower.
p3: The collapse of the USSR ended the Cold War definitively. It was the most dramatic geopolitical change since the end of WWII — 15 new states, the disappearance of the second superpower, and the triumph of capitalism over communism as the world's dominant economic system.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What challenges did Russia face under Yeltsin?
p1: Yeltsin introduced 'shock therapy' — rapid transition to a market economy. Price controls were removed overnight in January 1992, causing hyperinflation. State industries were privatised rapidly but corruptly — 'oligarchs' acquired vast state assets at far below true value.
p2: Political instability: in October 1993 hard-line communists barricaded themselves in the Russian parliament — Yeltsin ordered tanks to shell the building, killing at least 187 people. In December 1994 Yeltsin launched a military campaign in Chechnya — Russian forces suffered humiliating defeats.
p3: By the mid-1990s Yeltsin's health was failing, Russia had lost its superpower status and its international influence was a fraction of the USSR's. Yeltsin resigned on 31 December 1999, handing power to his chosen successor Vladimir Putin.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What caused the collapse of Yugoslavia?
p1: Yugoslavia had been a unique communist state — Tito resisted Stalin and maintained independence. After Tito's death in 1980 the federation began to fracture. Serbian nationalist Slobodan Milosevic became president of Serbia in 1989 and promoted Serbian interests across Yugoslavia.
p2: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in June 1991 — war broke out immediately. In Bosnia a three-way conflict between Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats led to the worst violence in Europe since WWII. Serbian forces conducted 'ethnic cleansing'. The Srebrenica massacre (July 1995) saw 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys murdered.
p3: NATO bombing campaigns against Serbia in 1995 forced the Dayton Peace Agreement. Yugoslavia showed the dangerous consequences of communism's fall in multi-ethnic states — when the communist framework suppressing ethnic nationalism was removed, old rivalries re-emerged with catastrophic force.
